docs.title: Automation with n8n 👋
docs.text:
Welcome. This module is 12 hours over 4 sessions. You will learn to build automated workflows and AI agents with n8n.

At the end you build your own project, alone, and you present it.

You always work alone

There are no teams in this module. Every session is individual work. You help each other, but each person has their own n8n instance and their own project.

docs.title: The 4 sessions
docs.text: Session Time What happens Séance 1 — Introduction and workflows 3 h What automation is. The n8n interface, nodes, tools. You build 5 workflows, no AI yet. Guided exercises. Séance 2 — Agent-oriented workflows 3 h How an AI agent works inside a workflow. You add AI steps, then a real AI Agent node. Guided exercises. Séance 3 — Project launch 2 h You pick your own real use case and start building a production-quality agent workflow. 2 weeks — Autonomous work. You build your project alone. Séance 4 — Soutenance 3–4 h You present your workflow, explain how it works, and justify why it is useful. This is the exam.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Your grade comes from the project + the soutenance. Two things are graded:

  1. How it works — you can explain every step of your own workflow.
  2. Why it is relevant — you can justify the use case and your design choices.

Details on the project brief and the soutenance guide arrive in Séance 3 and 4.

docs.title: Your tools
docs.text: What Where Your n8n instance URL + login given in Séance 1. It is YOUR space. Nobody else works in it. This site All exercise instructions. Keep it open next to n8n. The survival card Vocabulary + the 5 useful formulas. Open it here. Slack Ask questions in #test-seance-1. Your workflows will also send messages there.

docs.title: 🚚 FoodFleet — the demo company
docs.text:
In Séance 1 and 2, every exercise uses the same fake company: FoodFleet.

FoodFleet is a small B2B startup. It delivers lunches to offices. It has normal problems: watch competitor menus and prices, catch new leads from a web form, sort customer feedback, build the daily order list, send a weekly report.

You do not invent a use case in Séance 1 and 2. You work on FoodFleet, like a new engineer joining the company. This keeps the focus on n8n itself.

From Séance 3 you stop using FoodFleet. You choose your own project.

docs.title: 3 rules
docs.text:
Rule 1 — Nobody touches your keyboard

Someone helps you? They point at the screen and explain. YOU type. This is how you really learn it.

Rule 2 — Try 3 things first

Stuck? In order: 1) re-read the step and open the next hint, 2) ask your neighbour, 3) search the error message. Then raise your hand.

Rule 3 — This cohort moves fast

You are engineering and AI students. The exercises below were written for a less technical audience, so the pace here is faster. We skip the long explanations about JSON and HTTP. If an explanation feels obvious, it is: skip it and go to the next checkpoint.

docs.title: How an exercise page works
docs.text:
Every exercise page has the same shape:

  • A Goal line: what works at the end.
  • CP1, CP2, CP3… = checkpoints. Small steps. Each one ends with ✅ Done when: a thing you can see on screen.
  • Hints in closed boxes. Open them one by one, only when you are stuck. The last hint is usually the answer.
  • Some exercises contain one planted bug. Finding it is part of the exercise.

docs.title: n8n survival card
docs.text: Keep this tab open next to n8n. All the vocabulary of the module is here.

docs.title: Words
docs.text: Word What it means Node One box on the canvas = one step ("fetch this", "send that") Workflow The whole chain of boxes, left to right Trigger The node that starts the workflow (a clock, a form, an event) Webhook A URL. When something outside calls it, your workflow starts API A door a service opens, so your workflow can ask it for data JSON The data format: objects inside objects, each with a key Payload The data that just arrived Field A key and its value in the JSON (name: "Camille") Item One record of data. A node can process 1 item or 200 items in one run Credential A login or key stored in n8n. You select it from a list. You never retype it Expression A formula field. Anything inside {{ }} is replaced by real data Execution ONE run of your workflow. Click it to see what each step did Filter / IF A node that lets some items pass and blocks the others Merge A node that joins two streams of data into one Rate limit The API says "too many calls, slow down". Wait, or space out the calls LLM Chain An AI node that always does the same thing: prompt in, text out Agent An AI node with a mission and tools. It decides by itself what to call, and in what order Tool A capability you plug into an Agent — read a sheet, call an API. The agent chooses to use it or not

docs.title: The 5 useful formulas
docs.text:
{{ $json.name }}
→ the name field from the previous node

{{ $json.company.city }}
→ a field inside a field

{{ $json.hits[0].title }}
→ the FIRST element of a list — lists start at 0

{{ $now.format('dd/MM') }}
→ today's date

{{ $json.email || "no email" }}
→ a fallback value when the field is empty

docs.title: The 2 reflexes
docs.text:
1. 🔴 Red node? Open it. Read the first line of the error. Only the first line.
  2. 🤔 Not sure of a field name? Open the previous node. Look at its OUTPUT panel. The answer is always there.

docs.title: One more thing about undefined
docs.text: A field name that does not exist does not give a red error. It gives an empty string. The node stays green. This is the most common bug in this module.

docs.title: 1.0 — Install n8n with Docker 🐳
docs.text:
Goal: n8n runs on your own laptop, in your browser, at localhost:5678.

Time: 15 minutes.

Mode: individual. Every student runs n8n locally, on their own machine. No shared server, no login card. This is one reason the module uses n8n: it is open source and self-hosted — your data stays on your computer, not on someone else's server.

Why Docker?

n8n needs Node.js, a database, and some configuration to run. Docker packages all of that into one container — an isolated, ready-to-run box. You do not install Node.js or anything else by hand. One command, and n8n is running.

docs.title: CP0 — Docker is installed and running
docs.text:
1. Open a terminal.
  2. Run: 
    docker --version
  3. You should see a version number, for example Docker version 27.x.x.

✅ Done when: the command prints a version, with no error. → CP0.

Hint — command not found

Docker is not installed. Install Docker Desktop:

  • Mac: docker.com/products/docker-desktop
  • Windows: same link. Docker Desktop needs WSL2 — the installer will tell you if it is missing, and offer to set it up. Accept, then restart your laptop.
  • Linux: install Docker Engine from your distribution's package manager (docker.io on Debian/Ubuntu), then add yourself to the docker group so you don't need sudo for every command: 
    sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
    Log out and back in for this to take effect.

Do this before the session if you can — a laptop install is slow on shared wifi.

Hint — Docker Desktop is installed but the command still fails

Docker Desktop must be running (the whale icon in your menu bar / system tray). Open the Docker Desktop app, wait for it to say "Docker Desktop is running", then try again.

docs.title: CP1 — Start n8n
docs.text:
Follow the official n8n Docker Compose guide: docs.n8n.io/hosting/installation/docker — it stays accurate as n8n changes, so we link to it instead of copying commands here. Use the Docker Compose steps on that page (not plain docker run): Compose remembers your data when you stop and restart n8n, and you'll be doing that all module.

Once you're through it:

  1. Check the container is running: 
    docker compose ps
    You should see one container, STATUS = Up.

✅ Done when: docker compose ps shows the container running. → CP1.

Hint — port 5678 already in use

Something else on your laptop is already using that port. Either stop it, or change the port mapping in your docker-compose.yml (e.g. "5679:5678"), restart with docker compose up -d, then open localhost:5679 instead in CP2.

Hint — first start is slow

The first run downloads the n8n image (a few hundred MB). This can take a minute or two depending on the wifi. Every start after that is instant.

docs.title: CP2 — Open n8n and create your owner account
docs.text:
1. Open http://localhost:5678 in your browser.
  2. n8n asks you to create the owner account for this instance: email, name, password. This accounts stays local to your machine — you are not registering on a server somewhere.
  3. Skip or complete the optional setup questions n8n asks on first launch — none of them matter for this module.
  4. You should land on an empty canvas with + Add first step.

✅ Done when: you see the empty n8n canvas. → CP2. Go to Ex 1.1.

Hint — blank page / connection refused

n8n is still starting. Wait 10 seconds and reload. Still nothing? Check docker compose logs -f n8n for an error, or raise your hand.

docs.title: Keep in mind for the rest of the module
docs.text:
• Stop n8n at the end of a session: docker compose stop (keeps your workflows for next time). Restart it: docker compose up -d. Do not use docker compose down -v — the -v deletes your saved data.
  • Your workflows, credentials, and executions all live in the n8n_data Docker volume on your laptop. Nobody else can see them. Back them up yourself if you care about them past the module (Settings → Download all workflows, or the n8n CLI's export commands).
  • From Séance 3 you will connect n8n to real external services (Slack, Google, an LLM provider, GitHub, …) using your own accounts. Today you only need n8n itself running — no credential except n8n's own owner login.

Finished early?

Click around. Double-click a node category in the search box, read what nodes exist. You cannot break anything — it is your own local instance, and nothing is connected yet.

docs.title: Ex 1.0 — Setup Sprint ⚙️
docs.text:
Goal: your environment works, and you have sent your first message from n8n.

Time: 20 minutes. Faster if nothing fights back.

Why a 'setup' exercise?

Connecting accounts is the first real obstacle in every automation project. So we treat it as an exercise, not as a chore. Checkpoints, hints, and then you move on.

docs.title: CP0 — Join the class Slack workspace
docs.text:
1. Open the invite link: join.slack.com/t/epita-n8n/shared_invite/zt-4djjazkr6-8qzp2OhhZo2r3ExTH7mOCA
  2. Create your account (any name is fine), join the Epita-n8n workspace.
  3. Go to the #test-seance-1 channel — that's where the credential links for CP2–CP4 below get posted, and where your bot messages land.

✅ Done when: you can see #test-seance-1 in your sidebar. → CP0.

docs.title: CP1 — Logged into your instance
docs.text:
1. Open http://localhost:5678 — the n8n you started in 1.0 — Install n8n (Docker).
  2. Log in with the owner account you created there.
  3. You should see the empty n8n canvas.

✅ Done when: you see "Start from scratch" or an empty canvas. → CP1.

Hint 1

Owner account not accepted? Check you are using the same email/password you set when n8n first opened. There is no "forgot password" on a fresh local instance — if you are truly stuck, stop the container and delete the volume to start over: docker compose down -v && docker compose up -d. You lose nothing, you have not built anything yet.

Hint 2

Still blocked after 2 tries? Raise your hand.

docs.title: Where your credentials come from
docs.text:
Three credentials, given to you in class — not pre-installed, because every student runs their own local n8n with nothing shared by default.

Slack and Google Sheets are class-shared accounts — one value for everyone, both in this one link:

privatebin.net/?e8981599c2dd4a14#AjwdJPyQQGFexj4FVNpFG2TjiNmNdTYFgkuBGx5dnmDd

The password is given out loud in class, not written anywhere.

The LLM key is yours alone — one per student, $1 cap each, sent to you personally as a Slack DM, not posted in a channel. See CP4.

Open the link(s) right as you reach each part of the exercise below, copy the value straight into your own local n8n, now. Do not screenshot or save them anywhere else, and do not reuse them in your own projects — they get shut off once the module ends.

docs.title: CP2 — Your first workflow: a Slack message
docs.text:
We build the smallest possible workflow: 2 nodes, started by hand.

  1. Click + Add first step → search Manual Trigger → add it.
  2. Click the + on the right of the trigger → search Slack → choose Send a message.
  3. In the Slack node: Credential field → Create new credential. Choose Slack API, paste the Bot token from the class credentials link above (SLACK_BOT_TOKEN). At the top, rename the credential to exactly Workshop Slack — every later exercise and skeleton you import expects that exact name. Save.
  4. Channel: #test-seance-1 · Message: anything you want. Everyone can read it.
  5. Click Execute workflow at the bottom.

✅ Done when: your message appears in #test-seance-1. → CP2.

Hint 1

Slack node red? Open it, read the first line of the error (reflex 1 on your survival card). "Channel not found" means the channel name is wrong, or the bot was never invited to it — ask.

Hint 2

"Invalid auth" on save? You likely copied the token with a trailing space, or copied the wrong one (it starts with xoxb-). Re-open the class credentials link, copy again.

docs.title: CP3 — Google Sheets answers
docs.text:
1. New workflow (menu → New workflow).
  2. Add Manual Trigger, then a Google Sheets node → Get row(s) in sheet.
  3. Credential field → Create new credential. Choose Google Sheets Service Account, paste the service-account email (GOOGLE_SA_EMAIL) and private key (GOOGLE_SA_PRIVATE_KEY) — or the full JSON if your node only has one field — from the same class credentials link. Rename the credential to exactly Workshop Google — same reason as Slack. Save.
  4. Document: FoodFleet — Shared Sandbox · Sheet: Sheet1.
  5. Execute workflow. The OUTPUT panel should show a few test rows.

✅ Done when: you see data in OUTPUT. → CP3.

Hint 1

Document missing from the list, or a permission error? The service account needs to be shared on the sheet as an Editor — that is already done on the class copy. Re-check you pasted the whole JSON key, including the outer { }.

docs.title: CP4 — Add your LLM credential
docs.text:
The LLM key is different from the other two: it's yours alone, not shared with the class. Instead of one link for everyone, you get a Slack DM, sent to you personally, with one individual API key capped at $1.

  1. Check your Slack DMs for the link. Open it, copy the key.
  2. Left menu → Credentials → Create credential → OpenRouter.
  3. Paste your claimed API key. Rename the credential to exactly Workshop LLM — same reason as the other two. Save.
  4. Left menu → Credentials again. You should now see three: Workshop Slack, Workshop Google, Workshop LLM.

✅ Done when: all three are there. Do not edit or delete them — you need all three for the rest of the module. → CP4. Go to Ex 1.1.

Default model: openai/gpt-4o-mini

Use this model for the exercises unless told otherwise — it's cheap and its tool-calling works reliably with n8n's AI Agent node. You can try other models later once you understand the trade-offs (Séance 2 covers this).

Finished early?

Help a neighbour (rule 1: do not touch their keyboard). Or explore the canvas: double-click a node and look at its options. You cannot break anything. It is your own local instance.

docs.title: Ex 1.1 — Good Morning, Founder ☕
docs.text:
Goal: every morning at 9:00, a digest of food-industry news arrives in Slack by itself.

What you learn: scheduled triggers, calling an API, reading JSON, {{ }} expressions.

Context: the FoodFleet founder wants one short news digest every morning about her market. Today you build it for her.

🐛 This workflow has ONE bug — on purpose

You import a skeleton we prepared. It contains exactly one bug, in the "Format message" node. Finding it and fixing it is part of the exercise. Real workflows always arrive broken.

docs.title: Step 0 — Import the skeleton
docs.text:
1. Download good-morning-founder.json
  2. In n8n: ⋯ menu (top right) → Import from file → pick the file.
  3. You should see 4 nodes: Schedule Trigger → Get news (HTTP) → Format message → Slack.

docs.title: CP1 — The workflow runs
docs.text:
Click Execute workflow. Some nodes turn green. Maybe not all of them. That is normal at this stage.

✅ Done when: at least the first 2 nodes are green. → CP1.

docs.title: CP2 — Look at what the API returns
docs.text:
1. Open the Get news (HTTP) node. It calls the Hacker News search API: 
    https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search?query=fintech&tags=story
  2. Look at the OUTPUT panel. Find the hits list. Each element has a title, a url, and points.
  3. Replace fintech with a FoodFleet keyword: food delivery, foodtech, logistics, catering. Use one English word or two.
  4. Re-run the node.

✅ Done when: OUTPUT shows articles about the food or delivery market. → CP2.

Hint 1

OUTPUT empty, hits: []? Your keyword is too narrow. Use a broader English word. You need results for the next step. They do not have to be perfect.

docs.title: CP3 — Find and fix the bug 🐛
docs.text:
1. Open Format message. It builds the digest text with expressions: 
    ☀️ Good morning! Here is your FoodFleet digest for {{ $now.format('dd/MM') }}:
1. {{ $json.hits[0].titel }} → {{ $json.hits[0].url }}
2. {{ $json.hits[1].title }} → {{ $json.hits[1].url }}
3. {{ $json.hits[2].title }} → {{ $json.hits[2].url }}
  2. Run the workflow. Read the message it produces. One line is wrong.
  3. Fix it. (Reflex 2 on the survival card: the previous node shows you the real field names.)

✅ Done when: all 3 lines show a real title. Nothing empty. → CP3.

Hint 1

Compare line 1 with lines 2 and 3. Character by character.

Hint 2

A field that does not exist gives no red error. It gives an empty string. So everything is green and a piece of the sentence is simply missing. That is why this bug is nasty.

Hint 3 — the answer

In the API's JSON the field is called title. Line 1 asks for titel.

docs.title: CP4 — The digest arrives in Slack
docs.text:
1. Open the Slack node: credential Workshop Slack, channel #news, message = the output of Format message (already wired).
  2. Execute workflow → check Slack.

The skeleton arrives with the wrong channel

The imported JSON has #veille in the Slack node (leftover from another cohort). Change it to #news. Same thing in Ex 1.3.

✅ Done when: your digest is in #news. → CP4.

docs.title: CP5 — Schedule it for 9:00 tomorrow
docs.text:
1. Open Schedule Trigger → set: every day, 09:00.
  2. Top right of the canvas: switch the workflow to Active.

✅ Done when: the toggle is green / "Active". Tomorrow at 9:00 the digest arrives alone. → CP5. 🎉

Finished early?

  • Add the points of each article: {{ $json.hits[0].points }} pts
  • Two keywords at once. Read the API docs: query=foodtech%20OR%20catering
  • Build the list with a loop instead of three hardcoded lines. Look at the Split Out and Aggregate nodes. You will need them again in Ex 1.3 and 2.2.

docs.title: Ex 1.2 — Lead Landed 🔥
docs.text:
Goal: when a prospect fills the FoodFleet web form, a clean alert arrives in Slack within one second.

What you learn: webhooks (the opposite of a clock — here the outside world starts the workflow), field mapping, and above all building a workflow from nothing.

Context: FoodFleet has a "request a demo lunch" form on its website. Today nobody sees the submissions until someone opens the spreadsheet. You fix that.

🏗 Empty canvas — no skeleton this time

In 1.1 you repaired an existing workflow. Here you start from zero. You find, place and connect every node yourself. The screenshots show where you should arrive at each checkpoint. Only 3 nodes. You already know everything you need.

docs.title: CP1 — The webhook exists and listens
docs.text:
1. New workflow, name it Lead Landed.
  2. + Add first step → search Webhook → add it.
  3. Open the node. Copy the Test URL (copy button).
  4. Click Listen for test event. The node now waits, like a phone waiting for a call.

✅ Done when: the node shows that it is listening. → CP1.

docs.title: CP2 — A prospect calls your webhook
docs.text:
In production this URL is wired to the FoodFleet web form. Today, you are the prospect:

  1. Open a new tab. Paste your Test URL and add at the end: 
    ?name=Camille&company=Dataiku&budget=50000
    (any values you like — it is your dream customer)
  2. Press Enter. The tab shows a small response. In n8n, your webhook received the call.
  3. Look at the Webhook node's OUTPUT. Where are name, company, budget? Not at the top level. They are inside an object called query. Remember that path.

✅ Done when: you see your three values in OUTPUT, under query. → CP2.

Hint 1

Nothing received? Check two things: the node was on Listen for test event BEFORE you opened the URL, and you copied the Test URL, not the Production one.

docs.title: CP3 — The clean alert goes to Slack
docs.text:
1. Add a Slack → Send a message node after the webhook. Credential Workshop Slack, channel #leads.
  2. Write the message with expressions. Your turn. Expected result: 
    🔥 New FoodFleet lead: Camille (Dataiku) — budget €50,000
  3. Execute the workflow (restart Listen for test event, then call the URL again).

✅ Done when: the alert arrives in #leads with the real values, not empty ones. → CP3.

Hint 1

Everything empty? Go back to the webhook OUTPUT (reflex 2). Is name directly in $json, or inside an object?

Hint 2

The path to a field inside a field is formula 2 on the survival card: {{ $json.query.name }}.

docs.title: CP4 — Make it permanent
docs.text:
1. Save. Switch the workflow to Active.
  2. The webhook's Production URL now works all the time. Send it to a neighbour and ask them to send you a fake lead.

✅ Done when: an alert arrives while the canvas is not even open. Your workflow runs without you. That is what automation means. → CP4. 🎉

Finished early?

  • Add an email field with a fallback: {{ $json.query.email || "not provided" }}
  • Add a third node: every lead is also written into your FoodFleet sandbox Google Sheet, one row per lead. That is the start of a real CRM.
  • Switch the webhook to POST and send the body with curl instead of query parameters. Where does the data appear in OUTPUT now?

docs.title: Ex 1.3 — Mention Radar 📡
docs.text:
Goal: when FoodFleet's market gets mentioned online, an alert arrives in Slack.

What you learn: polling (checking at regular intervals), filtering items with an IF node, and the worst kind of bug: the one with no error at all.

Context: the FoodFleet founder wants to know immediately when a competitor or the market is mentioned. Not tomorrow morning. Now.

🐛 This skeleton has ONE bug — in the 'Filter' node

Special feature: this bug gives no red node. The workflow runs green, and sends nothing, ever. This is the most dangerous bug in automation: silent success. Good hunt.

docs.title: Step 0 — Import the skeleton
docs.text:
mention-radar.json → Import from file.

5 nodes: Schedule Trigger → Search mentions (HTTP) → Split Out → Filter (IF) → Slack.

docs.title: CP1 — Mentions arrive
docs.text:
1. Open Search mentions (HTTP). It asks for the newest stories: 
    https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search_by_date?query=fintech&tags=story
  2. Replace fintech with a FoodFleet keyword. Keep a common word for this exercise. You need enough results to test.
  3. Execute. The Split Out node turns the hits list into separate items. Look at its OUTPUT: it is no longer ONE response containing 20 articles, it is 20 items.

✅ Done when: Split Out outputs several items. → CP1.

docs.title: CP2 — The bug: nothing passes the filter 🐛
docs.text:
1. Execute the whole workflow. Everything is green, and #news stays empty. Nobody is notified of anything. A dead radar that reports "OK".
  2. Open the Filter (IF) node. It should let through articles whose title contains your keyword.
  3. Compare what the condition really says with what you want. Fix it.

✅ Done when: items come out of the filter's true branch. → CP2.

Hint 1

Look at the operator of the condition. "The title IS this word" and "the title CONTAINS this word" are very different.

Hint 2

A title is almost never one single word. is equal to will never match a full title against foodtech. Find the contains operator in the list.

Hint 3 — think about it

How do you catch this class of bug in production, when nobody is watching? One answer: an inverse alert — "I have sent nothing for 3 days, that is suspicious". Keep this idea. Your Séance 3 project needs a failure case, and this is a good one.

docs.title: CP3 — The alert goes out
docs.text:
true branch → Slack node, message with title and URL. Execute.

The skeleton's Slack node arrives set to #veille — change it to #news, like in Ex 1.1.

✅ Done when: alerts arrive, and only for relevant articles. → CP3.

docs.title: CP4 — Turn the radar on
docs.text:
Schedule every 30 minutes → Active.

✅ Done when: it is green. Your radar runs. → CP4. 🎉

And the real problem with polling?

Your radar sends you the same articles every 30 minutes. Annoying. That problem — "what is actually NEW?" — is exactly the subject of Ex 1.4. Want to look ahead? Open the Remove Duplicates node and read its option to remember state between runs.

docs.title: Ex 1.4 — The Two Spreadsheets 🧹
docs.text:
Goal: new FoodFleet sign-ups in spreadsheet A are copied into the CRM (spreadsheet B), without ever creating a duplicate.

What you learn: the item model, comparing two datasets, idempotence, and one universal truth: real data is dirty.

Level: the hardest exercise of Séance 1. If you finish it, you have understood the most subtle concept in n8n.

🐛 No hidden bug this time — the DATA is the bug

The skeleton is clean. But the spreadsheets are filled like real life: duplicates, random capitalisation (ACME vs Acme), invisible trailing spaces, one half-empty row. Your workflow must survive that. No hint tells you where the traps are. Open the data and LOOK at it. That is the skill of this exercise.

docs.title: Step 0 — Import
docs.text:
deux-tableurs.json → 4 nodes, all disconnected: Manual Trigger, Read A (sign-ups), Read B (CRM), Add to B.

All the wiring is missing. That is your job, starting with the Trigger to both reads (Trigger → Read A AND Trigger → Read B: one output going to two nodes).

Your two test tabs are in the shared FoodFleet — Shared Sandbox document: 1.4 — Inscriptions (the sign-ups) and 1.4 — CRM. The skeleton's two read nodes already point at them.

Why a Manual Trigger here, when 1.1 and 1.3 did not need one?

Here you wire two different reads into the same node (Compare Datasets). If you run Read A then Read B separately with each node's Execute step button, n8n keeps only one result in memory at a time: the second overwrites the first. The Manual Trigger plus the Execute workflow button re-runs both reads in the same pass, so Compare Datasets receives both fresh results at once.

docs.title: CP1 — You can see both datasets
docs.text:
Wire Trigger → Read A and Trigger → Read B. Click Execute workflow (not Execute step on each node — read the box above if you are not sure why).

Look at the OUTPUT of Read A and Read B. How many sign-ups? How many already in the CRM? Find with your eyes what will cause trouble. There are at least 3 traps.

✅ Done when: you can say out loud which rows of A are really new. → CP1.

docs.title: CP2 — The machine compares them
docs.text:
1. Find the Compare Datasets node. Wire Read A and Read B into it.
  2. Comparison field: email. It is the least bad identifier. Names are spelled differently every time.
  3. Execute workflow (from the trigger, not node by node). Look at the node's 4 outputs. The one you want: "In A only" = the real new sign-ups.

✅ Done when: "In A only" contains items. → CP2. But check the count: is it RIGHT? (Probably not. See CP3.)

Hint 1

The node asks for two inputs, A and B. The order matters. A = the source, B = what already exists.

docs.title: CP3 — Getting the count right (normalisation)
docs.text:
MARIE@acme.fr and marie@acme.fr are the same person for you. Not for a computer. You must normalise before comparing:

  1. Insert an Edit Fields node after each read (A and B).
  2. Rewrite email in a clean form: lowercase, no spaces. Two chained functions: 
    {{ $json.email.toLowerCase().trim() }}
  3. Execute workflow again. The count in "In A only" should now match what you counted with your eyes in CP1.

✅ Done when: the machine's count = your human count from CP1. → CP3.

Hint 1

Count by hand first: how many rows of A have an email that truly does not exist in B, once you ignore capitalisation and spaces? That number is your target.

Hint 2

The row with no email at all? Decide its fate explicitly (a Filter before the comparison: email is not empty). An automation that does not decide will crash one day, at the worst moment.

docs.title: CP4 — The sync runs twice
docs.text:
1. Wire "In A only" → Add to B. Execute: the new rows enter the CRM.
  2. The real test: run the whole workflow a SECOND time.

✅ Done when: the second run adds NOTHING (0 items in "In A only"). That is what "no duplicates" really means: not "it worked once", but "I can run it a thousand times". → CP4. 👑

This is the pattern you will reuse most

Read two sources, normalise, compare, write only the difference, stay safely re-runnable. This is the skeleton of half the automations that exist in companies. You just built it.

Keep it in mind for Séance 3: idempotence is one of the easiest ways to make your project look production-quality.
